result: The Digital Brain Bank is an open-access platform providing 21 whole-brain post-mortem MRI datasets organized into three themes (Digital Neuroanatomist, Digital Brain Zoo, Digital Pathologist), with data from 45 brains including diffusion MRI and complementary microscopy.
evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C18-C21, C29, C71-C72, and C75 collectively describe the Digital Brain Bank's structure, content, and scope. The manuscript provides clear documentation of the resource's organization, the number of datasets (21 whole-brain datasets from 45 brains), and the three thematic categories. This is a straightforward descriptive result about the resource itself.

result: The Human High-Resolution Diffusion MRI-PLI dataset provides one of the highest-resolution whole-brain human diffusion MRI datasets at 500 μm isotropic resolution, revealing anatomical details hidden at lower resolutions (1 mm, 2 mm) and showing agreement with complementary PLI data at 4 μm resolution.
evaluation: Claims C4, C27, C30-C35 describe the high-resolution dataset and its validation. The 500 μm resolution is documented, visual comparisons at multiple resolutions are shown in Figure 1, and agreement with PLI is demonstrated. The claim of 'one of the highest-resolution' is supported by the technical specifications and comparison with cited literature (C16).

result: The Digital Brain Zoo provides whole-brain diffusion MRI datasets from 14 nonhuman primate species spanning multiple taxonomic ranks, focusing primarily on diffusion MRI for comparative neuroanatomy investigations.
evaluation: Claims C5, C24, C47-C48 describe the nonhuman primate datasets. Table 1 documents the 14 species, Figure 2a shows the taxonomic coverage, and the text clearly states the focus on diffusion MRI. The data availability and species list are well-documented.

result: The Human ALS MRI-Histology dataset provides one of the largest post-mortem whole-brain cohort studies in neurodegeneration, with multimodal MRI and histology in 12 ALS and 3 control brains, revealing fractional anisotropy changes in the corpus callosum associated with motor and prefrontal regions.
evaluation: Claims C6, C26, C53-C58 describe the ALS cohort dataset. The cohort size (12 ALS, 3 control) is documented in Table 1 and text. The multimodal MRI and histology markers are specified (C54-C56). The FA analysis (C57) is shown in Figure 3c with statistical significance indicated, and agreement with prior literature (C58, Chapman et al., 2014) is cited. However, the claim of 'one of the largest' lacks quantitative comparison with other studies.

result: The Human Callosum MRI-PLI-Histology dataset provides diffusion MRI at 400 μm, PLI at 4 μm, and histology at 0.25 μm resolution in three excised human corpus callosum samples.
evaluation: Claims C36-C39 describe the corpus callosum dataset specifications. The resolutions and sample number are clearly stated in the text and Table 1, with citation to the original publication (Mollink et al., 2017). This is a straightforward descriptive result.

result: Tview is a bespoke web-based viewer enabling real-time visualization and interaction with MRI and microscopy data across drastically different spatial scales, using leafletjs technology with tiled image rendering.
evaluation: Claims C22-C23, C66-C68, C140-C142 describe Tview's development and functionality. The technical implementation (leafletjs, tiling approach) is documented, code availability is stated (C68), and the purpose (cross-scale visualization) is clear. The functionality claims are supported by the technical description.

result: Post-mortem tissue preserved with aldehyde solutions exhibits short relaxation times (T1, T2, T2*) and low diffusivity compared to in vivo tissue, making diffusion MRI particularly challenging.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81, C82, C103 describe the MR properties of fixed tissue. These claims are extensively supported by multiple citations to published literature (Birkl et al., Dawe et al., Shepherd et al., and others). This represents established knowledge in the field, well-documented in the manuscript.

result: The lab developed DW-SSFP methodology for high-SNR diffusion imaging in large post-mortem samples, which is well-suited to fixed tissue and demonstrates improved SNR-efficiency compared to conventional DW-SE, though the signal lacks a well-defined b-value requiring specialized processing.
evaluation: Claims C105-C107, C109, C111-C112 describe the DW-SSFP methodology. The development is documented with citations to the lab's publications (McNab et al., Miller et al., Foxley et al., Tendler et al.). The SNR advantages and b-value limitations are supported by cited literature. The transformation approach for human datasets (C112) is described with citations.

result: All samples were chemically fixed with aldehyde solutions; nonhuman brains and tissue blocks were soaked in PBS to increase SNR, but this was not performed in whole human brains due to the extended time required for penetration.
evaluation: Claims C87-C91 describe sample preparation protocols. The fixation and PBS soaking procedures are clearly documented with citations supporting the rationale (Shepherd et al., 2009 for SNR increase; Dawe et al., 2009 and others for penetration time). The experimental design decisions are justified.

result: Samples were imaged in proton-free susceptibility-matched fluid to minimize artifacts and field-of-view requirements; a custom two-stage holder was developed for whole human brains to ensure consistent positioning and minimize field inhomogeneities.
evaluation: Claims C92-C97 describe the scanning setup. The use of proton-free fluid and its advantages are documented (C92-C93). The custom holder design is described with reference to Appendix 3-figure 1, and its features (spherical cavity, consistent positioning) are explained with citation for B0-orientation effects (Liu, 2010).

result: Structural MRI in fixed tissue was acquired using bSSFP or T2-weighted sequences rather than conventional T1-weighted protocols, as T1 convergence in fixed tissue leads to poor contrast; these sequences provide excellent gray/white matter contrast with reversed appearance compared to in vivo T1-weighted images.
evaluation: Claims C98-C102 describe structural MRI methodology. The T1 convergence problem is cited (Miller et al., 2011), the sequence choices are documented in Table 1, and the contrast properties are based on established MRI physics. The high SNR-efficiency of bSSFP enabling ultra-high resolution is supported by the known properties of the sequence.

result: The group developed TIRL, a novel MR-microscopy coregistration toolbox that can be automated for 3D-to-2D registration and is specifically designed to handle deformations from histological processing; coregistrations are available for released histology in the ALS dataset with remaining data under curation.
evaluation: Claims C127, C147-C154 describe TIRL development and application. The toolbox is documented with citation (Huszar et al., 2019), its capabilities are described, and the rationale for 2D presentation (C150-C153) is explained based on the geometric constraints of histological processing. Data availability is clearly stated (C148-C149).

result: Diffusion datasets provide derived diffusivity estimates (diffusion tensor and/or ball-and-sticks parameters); human DW-SSFP datasets were transformed to well-defined b-values, but this was not possible for nonhuman datasets, which are recommended primarily for tractography investigations.
evaluation: Claims C110, C113-C117 describe data processing and limitations. The provision of derived parameters is documented (C110), the transformation approach for human datasets is cited (Tendler et al., 2020a,b), and the limitations for nonhuman datasets are clearly stated. The recommendation for tractography use (C115) is appropriately conservative given the b-value limitations.

result: Quantitative T1 and T2 maps are provided with human datasets using conventional sequences; T2 maps used EPG fitting to account for B1-inhomogeneity at 7T; T2* and susceptibility maps are available in a subset of ALS dataset brains.
evaluation: Claims C118-C123 describe quantitative mapping. The sequences and processing methods are documented with citations (Weigel, 2015 for EPG; Tendler et al., 2021 for T2; Wang et al., 2020 for T2*/susceptibility). The data availability is clearly stated in Table 1 footnote.

result: MRI data for all 12 ALS and 3 control brains are immediately available with a subset of histology data; remaining histology and MRI-histology coregistrations are being actively curated for future release.
evaluation: Claims C59-C63 describe data availability for the ALS dataset. The immediate availability of MRI data is stated (C61), partial histology availability is documented (C62), and ongoing curation is clearly indicated (C63). This is a straightforward statement about current and planned data releases.

result: Post-mortem MRI occupies a unique position in neuroscience, enabling high-resolution imaging, cross-species comparisons, and integration with microscopy while sharing signal mechanisms with in vivo MRI and tissue state with microscopy.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C17 provide background on post-mortem MRI capabilities. These are well-established principles in the field, supported by multiple citations to published literature. The claims represent accepted knowledge about the advantages and applications of post-mortem MRI rather than novel findings.

result: Post-mortem MRI enables scanning of species difficult to study in vivo, can be performed on whole brains with minimal handling, and facilitates formal comparisons of brain organization across species to identify homologies and principles of neural diversity.
evaluation: Claims C40-C46 describe advantages of post-mortem MRI for comparative neuroanatomy. These are supported by citations to published literature (Berns and Ashwell, Mars et al., Friedrich et al.) and represent established applications of the technique rather than novel findings.

result: MRI clinically lacks specificity to disease mechanisms as neurological diseases involve cellular-level changes below MRI resolution, but MRI contrast can be made sensitive to cellular phenomena, enabling correlation with histology in the same tissue.
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 describe the rationale for MRI-histology studies. These represent established knowledge about MRI limitations and the principle of cross-modality validation. The claims provide context for the Digital Pathologist datasets.

result: Few available viewers support both MRI and microscopy file formats, and single 2D microscopy images can exceed 10 billion pixels, creating barriers for data access and visualization.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 describe the motivation for Tview development. While the file size claim (C65) is reasonable based on microscopy specifications, the claim about viewer availability (C64) lacks systematic comparison with existing tools. No survey or quantitative assessment of available viewers is provided.

result: The Digital Brain Bank has flexible criteria for data inclusion, primarily providing pre-processed outputs to reduce user burden, with datasets associated with University of Oxford researchers and requiring ethical approval.
evaluation: Claims C69-C70, C155-C163 describe data policies. The inclusion criteria, ethical requirements, and data types provided are clearly stated. The rationale for pre-processed outputs is explained with citations to specialized methods (Tendler et al., Weigel).

result: The Digital Brain Bank will continue to grow with datasets under preparation, will be the primary release platform for new projects, and is anticipated to complement existing neuroimaging resources like the Human Connectome Project, PRIME-DE, and Brain Catalogue.
evaluation: Claims C28, C73-C74, C76-C79, C130-C135 describe future plans and anticipated impact. While ongoing datasets are cited (C28, C131-C132, C135), the claims about future growth (C73-C74) and complementarity with existing resources (C76-C79) are speculative. The integration and impact remain to be demonstrated.

result: Small samples were scanned on preclinical systems with powerful gradients using DW-SE; larger brains requiring human scanners with lower gradient strengths were addressed by developing alternative sequences (DW-SSFP) to increase SNR.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86, C108 describe the experimental strategy. The physical constraints (C84) and technical specifications (C85) are based on scanner capabilities. The methodological approach (C86, C108) is documented in Table 2 and supported by the DW-SSFP development described in other claims.

result: Post-mortem MRI-microscopy experiments are routinely used for validation but often restricted to summary statistics rather than pixel-wise comparisons; more detailed approaches are facilitated by accurate coregistrations.
evaluation: Claims C124-C126 describe common practices and challenges in the field. These are supported by citations (Mollink et al., 2017; Huszar et al., 2019; Iglesias et al., 2018) and represent established knowledge about MRI-microscopy integration.

result: NiiVue, a web-based 3D volumetric viewer, is being integrated for MRI-only dataset visualization and will support binary overlays to show tissue sampling locations.
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 describe ongoing development work. While NiiVue is cited (Rorden et al., 2021), the integration is stated as 'currently' happening (C128) and the overlay feature is described with 'will be used' (C129), indicating incomplete implementation. The functionality has not been demonstrated.

result: The Digital Brain Bank is a web application built with open-source software (Docker, Vue, leafletjs), hosted on local servers, with code available and an administration layer under development.
evaluation: Claims C136-C139, C143-C144 describe technical implementation. The technologies used are clearly stated, code availability is documented (C144), and ongoing development is indicated (C143). This is a straightforward description of the technical infrastructure.

result: The Digital Brain Bank is designed to work with associated publications for methodology details, provides pre-processed outputs to reduce user burden, and includes raw microscopy images with coregistered data under curation.
evaluation: Claims C145-C146, C164-C173 describe the data documentation and provision strategy. The approach is clearly stated, with rationale provided for pre-processed outputs (C164) and different treatment of DW-SE vs DW-SSFP data (C165-C168). Ongoing curation is indicated (C172).

result: Datasets will be updated over time with users contacted directly; future plans include streamlined access with user authentication, programmatic interfaces, detailed versioning, and DOI association.
evaluation: Claims C174-C178 describe current practices (C175) and future development plans (C176-C178). While the current notification approach is stated, the future features (authentication, programmatic access, versioning, DOIs) are aspirational and not yet implemented. These represent planned rather than achieved functionality.
